blocks.text: Chilliwack Farms: what the ground is and what governs it

What Chilliwack farm acreage actually is: whole fee-simple farm parcels across a city that is 67% agricultural land by the City's own statement — valley-floor farms under the AL and AS agricultural zones, upland farms under AU, farm-residential parcels under AR, and agricultural commercial / food-processing operations under AC and AFP. Tenure: farm parcels are overwhelmingly freehold; strata farm product is not a Chilliwack pattern (no strata farm complex was confirmed on an official source).

items.t: Minimum lot areas inside Section 6, zone by zone: AL and AU — 7.5 ha where land is excluded or exempted from the ALR or a subdivision is approved within the ALR, 1 ha if created by boundary adjustment to allow the more efficient use of agricultural land, and 0.2 ha if created by homesite severance or a boundary adjustment approved by the ALC (ss. 6.01(2), 6.02(2)); AS — 2 ha where a subdivision is approved in the ALR, 1 ha by boundary adjustment, and 0.2 ha by an ALC-approved boundary adjustment or homesite severance, or by subdivision of ALCA-exempt land served by a community water system (s. 6.03(2)); AR — 0.2 ha where served by a community water system, 1 ha for all other uses (s. 6.04(2)); AC — 2 ha (excluded/exempted or approved subdivision), 1 ha by boundary adjustment served by a community water system, and 0.2 ha by ALC-approved homesite severance (s. 6.05(2)); AFP — 0.4 ha for all uses (s. 6.06(2)). Minimum lot width is 25 m in all six zones. These are creation minimums keyed to the approval route — not surveyed sizes for any parcel, and no typical farm size is claimed beyond them.

Farm Home Plate figures inside Section 6: in the AL, AR and AC zones the Farm Home Plate is capped, as maximum lot coverage, at 4,000 m² for the principal residential use and 1,000 m² for an additional residential use (ss. 6.01(5), 6.04(5), 6.05(5)); the dwelling must be sited no farther than 70 m from the front or exterior side lot line with no part of the plate more than 80 m from that line, or no farther than 50 m from the rear lot line with the plate within 60 m (ss. 6.01(8), 6.04(8), 6.05(8)); and the Farm Home Plate requirements do not apply where a lot is under 0.8 ha in area (ss. 6.01(10), 6.04(10), 6.05(10)). The AU, AS and AFP sections state no Farm Home Plate figure. The OCP carries Development Permit Area 4 – Farm Home Plate, and a Development Permit is required when the Farm Home Plate regulations in the Zoning Bylaw are not met.
Soil: no agricultural capability class for Chilliwack's farm districts was confirmed from a text source: Not verified for any specific district or parcel class.

Governing bylaws: City of Chilliwack Zoning Bylaw 2020, No. 5000 — its Section 6 sets the agricultural zones: AL (Agricultural Lowland), AU (Agricultural Upland), AS (Agricultural Small Lot), AR (Agricultural Residential), AC (Agricultural Commercial) and AFP (Agricultural Food Processing); the OCP is Chilliwack 2050 (Bylaw No. 5500), with the Agricultural Plan at Schedule B1.

blocks.text: Local rules that affect acreage buyers

items.t: Zoning: Chilliwack Zoning Bylaw 2020, No. 5000, Section 6: establishes the AL, AU, AS, AR, AC and AFP agricultural zones (ss. 6.01–6.06), and Section 7 the rural zones including R (Rural) and RH (Rural Hillside). Read the exact agricultural zone, not just "farm": a small-lot (AS) purchase and a lowland (AL) purchase are different products with different subdivision and use rules (minimums).

The Farm Home Plate has a geography, not just a size cap: In the AL, AR and AC zones the dwelling must sit no farther than 70 m from the front or exterior side lot line (plate within 80 m), or no farther than 50 m from the rear lot line (plate within 60 m) — and the plate rules fall away entirely on lots under 0.8 ha. A house plan drawn for the middle of a large lowland parcel can fail the plate before it fails any size test.

The same 0.2 ha minimum means four different things in Section 6: A 0.2 ha lot is reachable by homesite severance or ALC-approved boundary adjustment in AL/AU, by ALC-approved severance or community-water subdivision of exempt land in AS, as the standard community-water minimum in AR, and by ALC-approved homesite severance in AC — the approval route, not the number, is what a buyer is actually purchasing.

The Agricultural Commission is built into the approval path: The Agricultural Area Plan was created in 2012 in partnership with the Chilliwack Agricultural Commission, and the Agricultural and Rural Advisory Committee (ARAC) monitors its implementation by reviewing agricultural development applications — farm applications in Chilliwack are reviewed through an agricultural lens by design.
No agricultural capability class for any Chilliwack farm district was confirmed from a text source, so capability for a specific parcel stays not verified until its own soil/ALC record is read.

Chilliwack farm ground surrounds the urban core across the valley floor and uplands. The City states agriculture accounts for 67% of the City's total land base and 29% of economic activity.

The Agricultural Land Reserve (ALR) covers about two-thirds of the city. The City's Official Community Plan material states the ALR occupies two-thirds of the municipality's land base and that farmland surrounds the city.
The City states the ALR is made up of the Fraser River valley bottom at about 14,000 hectares and Ryder Ridge at about 950 hectares.

The farm stock here is defined by six agricultural zones, not subdivisions. Zoning Bylaw 2020, No. 5000, Section 6 sets AL (Agricultural Lowland), AU (Agricultural Upland), AS (Agricultural Small Lot), AR (Agricultural Residential), AC (Agricultural Commercial) and AFP (Agricultural Food Processing) zones.

Minimum lot sizes differ sharply by zone and approval route. In AL and AU the minimum is 7.5 hectares for an ALR subdivision, 1 hectare by boundary adjustment, and 0.2 hectares by Agricultural Land Commission (ALC)-approved homesite severance or boundary adjustment.

Small-lot agriculture is a studied Chilliwack pattern. The City's Small Lot Agriculture Study states Chilliwack contains 41,862 acres in the ALR and that the City reviews applications for non-farm uses, exclusions, subdivisions and boundary adjustments.

blocks.text: Chilliwack Farms: rules that affect buyers

items.t: The Farm Home Plate limits where homes sit on farm land. In the AL, AR and AC zones the plate is capped at 4,000 square metres for the principal residential use and 1,000 square metres for an additional residential use, and Development Permit Area 4 applies where the plate rules are not met.

An ALC application may be needed before the City can approve farm building work. The City lists a new house, coach house or suite, placing fill or removing soil, non-farm uses, and subdivision or a boundary adjustment as items that may require an ALC application.

Floodplain building is regulated separately from zoning. Floodplain Regulation Bylaw 2018, No. 4519 sets setbacks of 60 metres from the Fraser River natural boundary, 75 metres from the Vedder River, and 30 metres from the Chilliwack River and Vedder Canal for buildings requiring floodproofing.

blocks.text: Chilliwack Farms: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: The Agricultural and Rural Advisory Committee (ARAC) reviews farm applications. The City states the Agricultural Area Plan was created in 2012 with the Chilliwack Agricultural Commission and ARAC monitors its implementation by reviewing agricultural development applications.

Check ALR status on the City Webmap before writing an offer. The City directs owners to use the City Webmap to check whether a property is in the ALR, and states ALC applications are referred to the City for review with its Letter of Authorization included.

Yarrow sits in two floodplains at once. The Yarrow Neighbourhood Plan states Yarrow is within the floodplains of both the Fraser River and the Vedder River, is protected by an extensive City-managed diking system, and a projected average flood depth of 4 metres applies if a dike fails.

Vedder River floods are mainly a fall and winter event. The City states larger Vedder River floods occur in fall and winter from heavy rainfall or rain-on-snow, while spring and summer rises come from snowmelt, and its Flood Response Plan is reviewed and updated every year.

Part of the ALR was underused in the last inventory cited by the City. The Small Lot Agriculture Study states an Agricultural Land Use Inventory in 2012 found over 1,400 hectares, or 8% of the ALR, underutilized and available with potential for farming.

Soils here are alluvial valley-bottom soils. A provincial report on the Chilliwack and Agassiz areas states agricultural soils developed on alluvial, lacustrine and glacial outwash materials, and most farms lie below 20 metres above sea level.

A leased-out farm parcel can lose class if the lease filing lapses. BC Assessment states a leased property is disqualified if a lease expires or seven years pass and a current lease is not submitted to the assessor by October 31 before the tax year.

Development application fees are set by bylaw. The City states its Development Application Fee Bylaw lists fees for all development applications and related services, which is the schedule to check for rezoning, development permit and ALR-related filings.
Highway 1 is the main route for farm goods and buyers.
Route 66 is a daily interregional service.

Route 71 links Chilliwack to Agassiz and Harrison Hot Springs. The FVRD states it administers Route 71 connecting Agassiz, Harrison Hot Springs and Chilliwack as one of its transit services delivered by BC Transit.

blocks.text: Chilliwack Farms: risks and due diligence

items.t: Flood risk covers most of the city outside the hillsides. The City's plan states that except for the hillsides and Sardis-Vedder area, Chilliwack is situated on floodplains, sharing Fraser River flood risk, with the Chilliwack and Vedder Rivers also presenting flood risk to portions of the community.

New building in the floodplain must meet flood construction levels. The Floodplain Regulation Bylaw requires habitable floor elevation at the applicable Flood Construction Level (FCL) for the Fraser, Chilliwack or Vedder River or Vedder Canal plus 0.6 metres freeboard in areas protected by a standard dike.
Confirm ALR status and whether an ALC application is needed for the intended use.

faq.a: On ALR land, one additional residence is permitted without an ALC application where the conditions are met — 90 m² or less on parcels of 40 ha or smaller, 186 m² or less on larger parcels — and City bylaws must also permit it; a secondary suite is permitted only inside the principal residence. The City lists a new house, coach house or suite among the items that may need an ALC application.
faq.q: Can a Chilliwack farm have a second dwelling?

faq.a: Only with the licence position confirmed: non-domestic groundwater use (irrigation is the example) requires a water licence under the Water Sustainability Act, with fees and rentals, before the water can lawfully be used; domestic use is exempt. Check the licence on any farm that irrigates from a well.
faq.q: Is the farm's water lawful to use for irrigation?

faq.a: Agriculture covers most of the city's land base. The City states agriculture accounts for 67% of the total land base and 29% of economic activity, and its plan material adds that farming in Chilliwack produces 10% of British Columbia's agricultural production on about 17,000 hectares, so farm neighbours and farm traffic are the normal setting, not an exception.
faq.q: How much of Chilliwack is actually farmed?

faq.a: The Farm Home Plate clusters the home so the rest stays farmable. The City states Development Permit Area 4 – Farm Home Plate exists to reduce the long-term impact of residential uses on agricultural land, a development permit is required when the Zoning Bylaw plate regulations are not met, and the plate caps are 4,000 and 1,000 square metres.
faq.q: What is the Farm Home Plate and why does it matter?

faq.a: Subdivision is tightly limited inside the ALR. The Zoning Bylaw sets a 7.5-hectare minimum for an ALR subdivision in the AL and AU zones, with 0.2 hectares reachable only by an ALC-approved homesite severance or boundary adjustment, and the City confirms subdivision or a boundary adjustment may require an ALC application first.
faq.q: Can I subdivide a Chilliwack farm into small lots?

faq.a: Yes, farm class depends on actual production and an annual filing.
faq.q: Do I need to keep farming to keep the lower tax class?

faq.a: The City of Chilliwack states agriculture accounts for 67% of the City's total land base and 29% of its economic activity, and its Official Community Plan carries an Agricultural Area Plan for that land.
faq.q: How much of Chilliwack is farmland?

faq.a: Section 6 of Zoning Bylaw 2020, No. 5000 sets six agricultural zones: AL (Agricultural Lowland), AU (Agricultural Upland), AS (Agricultural Small Lot), AR (Agricultural Residential), AC (Agricultural Commercial) and AFP (Agricultural Food Processing).

A principal residence built without an ALC application must have a total floor area of 500 m² or less, with no more than 1,000 m² of fill placed for its construction; Chilliwack also applies its Farm Home Plate rules (Development Permit Area 4) to residential building on agricultural land.
